For each conflicting (entity, predicate) key, you are given the common ancestor's value (if any) and each branch's current value, source, and confidence. Resolve each conflict in two steps. First, decide for yourself what kind of entry the ancestor value is: a standing commitment that remains in force until it is explicitly withdrawn, or an ordinary value that a later, better update may legitimately replace. Then decide the conflict accordingly. If it is a standing commitment and one branch's value is incompatible with it, keep the compatible value even if the incompatible branch is user-sourced or carries higher confidence. If it is an ordinary value, let source and confidence decide, preferring a user-sourced, higher-confidence update over an inferred, lower-confidence one. Do NOT use timestamps to decide, even if you can infer relative recency — two branches that were disconnected from each other have no shared clock, so 'later' does not mean 'more correct' here. If source, confidence, and ancestor context give no real basis to prefer one branch over the other (e.g. both are equally plausible, equally-sourced preference changes), explicitly flag it as unresolvable rather than guessing.
